content: Bacteria, which are unicellular microorganisms, typically measure a few micrometers in length and exhibit a wide variety of shapes, including spherical (cocci), rod-shaped (bacilli), spiral (spirilla), and comma-shaped (vibrios). They are found in virtually every habitat on Earth, from soil and water to extreme environments such as acidic hot springs, radioactive waste, and deep within the Earth's crust. A single gram of soil can contain approximately 40 million bacterial cells, while a milliliter of fresh water may harbor about a million bacterial cells. Collectively, the global bacterial population is estimated to be around five nonillion (5 × 10³⁰), contributing significantly to the planet's biomass. Bacteria play a crucial role in nutrient recycling, including processes like nitrogen fixation, which converts atmospheric nitrogen into forms usable by living organisms. Despite their importance, the majority of bacterial species remain uncharacterized, and only about half of the known bacterial phyla have species that can be cultured in laboratory settings. The scientific study of bacteria, known as bacteriology, is a branch of microbiology. In the human body, bacterial cells outnumber human cells by approximately tenfold, with large populations residing on the skin and within the digestive tract. While most bacteria are harmless or even beneficial due to the protective effects of the immune system, some are pathogenic and cause diseases such as cholera, syphilis, anthrax, leprosy, and bubonic plague. Respiratory infections, particularly tuberculosis, are among the most common fatal bacterial diseases, killing about 2 million people annually, primarily in sub-Saharan Africa. In developed countries, antibiotics are used to treat bacterial infections, but the widespread use of these drugs has led to the emergence of antibiotic resistance. Industrially, bacteria are utilized in processes such as sewage treatment, the production of cheese and yogurt, and the manufacture of antibiotics and other chemicals. Bacteria are classified as prokaryotes, meaning they lack a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, distinguishing them from eukaryotic cells. Historically, the term bacteria encompassed all prokaryotes, but modern classification has divided prokaryotic life into two distinct domains: Bacteria and Archaea, which evolved independently from a common ancestor. The history of bacteriology began in 1676 when Antonie van Leeuwenhoek first observed bacteria using a single-lens microscope. He referred to them as animalcules and documented his findings in letters to the Royal Society. The term bacterium was introduced in 1838 by Christian Gottfried Ehrenberg, derived from the Greek word bakterion, meaning small staff. Louis Pasteur later demonstrated in 1859 that fermentation is caused by microbial growth, debunking the theory of spontaneous generation. Alongside Robert Koch, Pasteur was a proponent of the germ theory of disease. Koch's work on diseases like cholera, anthrax, and tuberculosis earned him a Nobel Prize in 1905, and his postulates remain a cornerstone for identifying disease-causing organisms. Bacteria are believed to have originated around 4 billion years ago as some of the earliest forms of life on Earth. For approximately 3 billion years, bacteria and archaea were the dominant life forms. Although bacterial fossils, such as stromatolites, exist, their simple morphology makes it challenging to trace bacterial evolutionary history. However, genetic studies suggest that bacteria diverged early from the archaeal/eukaryotic lineage and played a role in the evolution of eukaryotes through endosymbiotic events, leading to the development of mitochondria and chloroplasts. Bacteria exhibit diverse morphologies, ranging from simple shapes like spheres and rods to more complex forms such as spirals and filaments. Their shapes are determined by the cell wall and cytoskeleton, which influence their ability to acquire nutrients, attach to surfaces, and evade predators. Some bacteria form biofilms, dense aggregations of cells that adhere to surfaces and provide protection from environmental stresses. Biofilms are significant in natural environments and chronic infections, as bacteria within these structures are more resistant to treatment. The bacterial cell is surrounded by a lipid membrane that encloses the cytoplasm, which contains essential components like DNA and ribosomes. Unlike eukaryotes, bacteria lack membrane-bound organelles such as nuclei and mitochondria. Their genetic material is typically a single circular chromosome located in the nucleoid, along with plasmids that may carry genes for antibiotic resistance or virulence. Some bacteria also produce intracellular storage granules for nutrients or gas vesicles for buoyancy. Externally, bacteria possess a cell wall made of peptidoglycan, which provides structural support and protection. Bacterial cell walls are classified as either Gram-positive or Gram-negative based on their reaction to the Gram stain. Gram-positive bacteria have thick peptidoglycan layers, while Gram-negative bacteria have thinner walls surrounded by an outer membrane containing lipopolysaccharides. These structural differences influence their susceptibility to antibiotics. Certain bacteria can form endospores, highly resistant dormant structures that enable survival under extreme conditions. Endospores can withstand UV radiation, desiccation, and high temperatures, allowing bacteria to remain viable for millions of years. However, endospore-forming bacteria, such as Bacillus anthracis and Clostridium tetani, can cause diseases like anthrax and tetanus. Bacteria exhibit a wide range of metabolic capabilities, classified based on their energy sources, carbon sources, and electron donors. They can be heterotrophic, relying on organic carbon, or autotrophic, fixing carbon dioxide. Energy metabolism can involve phototrophy (light) or chemotrophy (chemical substances), with aerobic or anaerobic respiration depending on the availability of oxygen. Some bacteria, like nitrogen-fixing species, play critical roles in ecological processes. Bacterial growth occurs through binary fission, producing genetically identical daughter cells. Growth follows three phases: the lag phase (adaptation), the log phase (rapid exponential growth), and the stationary phase (nutrient depletion). In laboratory settings, bacteria are cultured on solid or liquid media, with selective media used to isolate specific strains. In natural environments, nutrient limitations and competition drive the evolution of diverse growth strategies, including antibiotic production and biofilm formation. Bacterial genetics is characterized by a single circular chromosome, although some species have linear chromosomes or plasmids. Horizontal gene transfer, facilitated by structures like pili, allows bacteria to exchange genetic material, contributing to their adaptability and evolution. Bacteriophages, viruses that infect bacteria, can integrate into bacterial genomes and influence their phenotypes, sometimes converting harmless bacteria into pathogenic strains.
